lesson.title: Two Railroads, One Nation: Building the Transcontinental Line
lesson.summary: In 1869 two railroad companies building from opposite ends of the country met in Utah, finally linking the Atlantic and Pacific coasts by rail and transforming how Americans moved, traded, and thought about distance.
lesson.body:
Before 1869, getting from New York to California meant months of travel: a dangerous overland wagon route, a long sea voyage around South America, or a combination of ship and a risky crossing at Panama. This was an obstacle to the vision of Manifest Destiny, the belief that the United States was meant to extend from coast to coast. A railroad spanning the continent would finally make that vision practical, tying the farms, mines, and cities of the West to the industrial and financial centers of the East.

Congress made the project possible with the Pacific Railway Act of 1862, signed by President Abraham Lincoln. With the South out of Congress during the Civil War, northern lawmakers could finally push through a plan that earlier sectional disputes had blocked. The act chartered two companies to build the line: the Union Pacific Railroad, which built westward from Omaha, Nebraska, and the Central Pacific Railroad, which built eastward from Sacramento, California. To pay for construction, the government gave both companies enormous land grants alongside the tracks and government bonds for every mile completed, an arrangement that built directly on financing methods already used for canals and earlier railroads during the Transportation Revolution.

The two crews faced very different challenges. The Central Pacific had to blast and tunnel through the granite of the Sierra Nevada, brutal and dangerous work performed largely by Chinese immigrant laborers, who made up the large majority of the Central Pacific workforce by the mid 1860s. The Union Pacific crossed flatter Great Plains terrain but faced conflicts with Native American nations whose land the railroad cut through, and it relied heavily on Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. Because each company earned more money and land for every mile built, both raced to lay track quickly, sometimes at the expense of quality and safety.

The two lines finally met at Promontory Summit in Utah Territory on May 10, 1869. Central Pacific president Leland Stanford drove a ceremonial golden spike to mark the joining of the rails, an event that telegraph operators announced to the country almost instantly. A trip that once took months could now be completed in about a week.

The transcontinental railroad reshaped the country's economy and geography. It opened western land to settlement and resource extraction, moved cattle, grain, and ore to eastern markets, and made the railroad corporation the model for large scale American business. It also set a pattern that would repeat across the Gilded Age: massive government subsidies combined with private enterprise, producing extraordinary growth alongside corruption, labor exploitation, and the displacement of Native peoples from land they had long inhabited.

The financing scheme itself became a source of scandal. Union Pacific insiders had set up a construction company called Credit Mobilier that billed the railroad, and ultimately the federal government, at inflated prices while funneling profits back to the same insiders, some of whom had also distributed shares to sitting members of Congress to discourage scrutiny. When journalists exposed the scheme in the early 1870s, it became one of the defining corruption scandals of the era, a reminder that the single line of track uniting the country economically had been built on both remarkable engineering achievement and significant financial abuse.
